svg.title: Reference chart of how glycolysis is regulated, in six panels. Glucose transporters: GLUT2 in liver and pancreatic beta cells, Km about 15 mM, not affected by insulin; GLUT4 in skeletal muscle and fat, Km about 5 mM, moved from vesicles to the cell surface when insulin binds its receptor; GLUT4 is near saturation at normal blood glucose, so uptake depends on how many transporters are in the membrane. Hexokinase and glucokinase: computed curves of rate as a fraction of Vmax against glucose from 0 to 20 mM, with the blood glucose range 4 to 8 mM shaded; hexokinase, Km 0.1 mM, is saturated at any blood glucose, is in every tissue and is inhibited by glucose-6-phosphate; glucokinase, in liver and beta cells, has a Km about 10 mM and a slightly sigmoidal curve, so its rate follows blood glucose and the liver stores the excess after a meal; it is not inhibited by G6P and insulin raises its amount. PFK-1, the rate-limiting and committed step: activated by AMP (energy low) and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate (insulin, liver), inhibited by ATP (energy high, at an allosteric site) and citrate (citric acid cycle backed up); glucagon lowers F-2,6-BP and slows PFK-1 in the liver. PFK-2 and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate: one liver protein with PFK-2 and FBPase-2 activities; when fed, insulin keeps it dephosphorylated, PFK-2 is active, F-2,6-BP rises, PFK-1 is on and FBPase-1 off, favouring glycolysis; when fasting, glucagon raises cAMP and PKA phosphorylates it, FBPase-2 is active, F-2,6-BP falls, PFK-1 slows and FBPase-1 is freed, favouring gluconeogenesis; the Haworth projection of beta-D-fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is drawn, a signal rather than an intermediate. Pyruvate kinase: feed-forward activation by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate from step 3; turned off by ATP and alanine and, in the liver, by glucagon through PKA phosphorylation, which saves PEP for making glucose; inherited deficiency starves red blood cells of ATP and causes hemolysis. Red blood cells and 2,3-BPG: bisphosphoglycerate mutase turns 1,3-BPG into 2,3-BPG and a phosphatase turns that into 3-PG, skipping the ATP-making phosphoglycerate kinase step; computed oxygen dissociation curves show more 2,3-BPG shifting hemoglobin saturation to the right, lowering oxygen affinity so tissues get more oxygen (altitude, anemia); red blood cells have no mitochondria and get all their ATP from glycolysis.
svg.text: Who takes glucose in, and the enzymes at the three irreversible steps that set how fast it runs.
